At the same time, Banxico recently revised its 2026 GDP forecast higher to 1.5% from 1.1% in its Q2 inflation report, but this still remains below Mexico's estimated potential growth rate, which we believe is closer to 2%. The implication is that any inflationary impact from currency weakness is likely to be partially offset by a negative output gap. That gives policymakers further justification to prioritize supporting growth rather than defending the currency. Financial Markets Show Little Sign of Panic. Perhaps equally important, financial markets have not responded to Banxico's dovish shift in a manner that would force a policy response. Our positioning data continue to show inflows into local bond markets even as MXN has weakened (Figure 5). Investors appear to be accepting currency weakness as a natural consequence of a less restrictive monetary policy stance. If markets believed Banxico's policy approach risked unanchoring inflation expectations or creating broader country-risk concerns, capital would likely be leaving the bond market. The opposite is occurring. This suggests policymakers face limited pressure from a financial stability perspective. records.text: sectors current fundamentals are not as robust due to a combination of rising operational costs and shifting structural pressures. Years of persistent labor shortages globally have driven up wages for nurses and clinical staff, squeezing hospital margins. At the same time, stricter regulatory oversight, patent expirations for major blockbuster drugs, and intense pricing scrutiny on pharmaceuticals have made it harder for companies to sustain high growth. This is evident when we are looking at how margins have evolved in recent years (Figure 4). A sector that once enjoyed stable margins is now seeing its profitability eroding, and the gap with the global market is widening. And it is not just margins. Return on equity (ROE) and cash flows are also seeing a declining trend. Figure 5: Future expectations are dire Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg This is the main reason why earnings have been guided lower, and Health Care is the only sector globally that is seeing negative earnings expectations for the rest of 2026 (Figure 5). But we should keep in mind that this is a very diverse sector. Healthcare equipment is very defensive, with low but stable margins, while Pharma tends to offer growth and higher profitability. Figure 6 shows that 2026’s contracting earnings are driven by Pharma companies. This could reflect the impact of the GLP-1 boom. records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General HEALTH CARE IS LAGGING BEHIND Health Care has underperformed since the beginning of the year, but has recently recovered some of the losses, as risk appetite started to deteriorate. Clients are frequently asking whether it is time to enter the sector, and cite three main reasons: (1) Health care is a defensive that offers quality growth, (2) it seems like a good hedge to Technology and (3) valuations and positions seem to have bottomed. After careful analysis, here are our answers along with a bonus section on Health Care’s credit state in public and private markets. 1. Is Health Care defensive enough? Defensive sectors, including Health Care, tend to do well during times of uncertainty due to their generally stable earnings profile . Demand for Health Care is largely independent from economic cycles and regardless of inflation, market volatility or geopolitical tension, individuals still require essential medical treatments, prescription drugs and emergency services. This consistent consumer need provides healthcare companies with stable cash flows, strong pricing power, and predictable earnings that few other industries can match. Figure 4: Margins have been consistently dropping Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg However, the sectors current fundamentals are not as robust due to a combination of rising operational costs and shifting structural pressures. Years of persistent labor shortages globally have driven up wages fo

ng emerges across IG Healthcare Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg In the same time period, HY spreads for US Health Care have tightened considerably. From a public credit perspective, the recent divergence between IG and HY markets shows that investors remain divided on the sector ’s outlook. This could be attributed to the diversity of companies, especially within the US sector. Private credit paints a much clearer picture of the risk associated with Health Care. The sector represents 18.63% of all BDC maturities through 2033. This equates to roughly $66.69b of the total $360.48b set to mature in the next several years (Figure 1 3). This means a significant refinancing burden still lies ahead for an industry that has struggled relative to others. Figure 13: Healthcare faces meaningful refinancing needs through 2033 Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg Also, Payment-In-Kind (PIK) usage remains elevated within Health Care compared to most sectors – the second highest contribution of any sectors behind Tech. At the same time, Health Care has the highest number of non -accruals of any sector by a large margin. PIK is commonly associated with future credit deterioration. Fitch noted that 41% of private credit defaults occurred through stressed maturity extensions, highlighting the refinancing challenges facing weaker borrowers. Marvin Loh 21 October 2026 1 Insights Classification: General, Complimentary Material DM FX Weekly : Organizing the Jenga blocks The market’s ability to ignore deleterious risk signals is facing its greatest test of the year. And while forks in the aggressive path of AI spend is again the market’s archnemesis, there is reason for us to be especially alert this time. We cite tightening financial conditions, credit stresses for weak borrowers and an extended risk-off posture for our real money investors. And while Treasuries are proving a safe haven, the USD and JPY are not responding in similar fashion. We are therefore lowering our exposure to the JPY, while maintaining our CHF long. This was true for the JPY and USD over the past few weeks, as we maintained two JPY longs against the NZD and AUD, a hedged regional approach to currency picking. We also instituted a EURUSD short earlier this month, as USD flows surged, while the EUR proved radioactive. The recent rise in volatility proved us correct, although FX has not performed as expected. In particular, we have seen haven demand re-emerge for Treasuries, with October rate hike expectations falling, easing upward pressure on yields, particularly at the long end after reaching multi-decade highs. We would therefore have expected our havens to perform well in this environment, although this was not the case. The decline in US yields proved idiosyncratic, with the recent fall in US real yields remaining within our borders. Figure 1 shows rising fixed income volati lity compressing cross border real yields differentials, narrowing the positive spread differentials against bunds and gilts. The USD smile was then more greatly influenced by rates rather than risk, with its historic correlations with equity vol remaining positive (counter to haven performance) even as treasury correlations returned to longer term averages (Figure 2). records.text: Anthi Tsouvali Macro Strategy Team 21 October 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Global Equity Strategy - Weekly Is it time to buy Health Care? This is one of the most frequent questions we get from clients currently, and the short answer is No! It is true that historically, Health Care has outperformed when risk appetite deteriorates, and has been a very good hedge to Tech. We do not believe that is the case now. The sectors fundamentals have weakened over the last 12 months, and we don’t yet see any signs that they have bottomed. We would stay away from Health Care. Risk appetite has recently dropped to negative territory (Figure 1) as investors worry that higher interest rates will put pressure on corporate profitably and equity outperformance could come to a halt. When uncertainty intensifies, investors typically demand more return for taking risk – higher term premium. Even as term premium has moved into positive territory, it remains historically low and could rise further. From an asset allocation perspective, this fear can be seen in investors ’ desire to shorten duration, and in equities , increasing allocations to lower -beta stocks that are less correlated with the gyrations of the market. Health Care is one sector that has historically done well in such an environment, and when term premiums initially rise, we see long only investors increase their allocation to Health Care stocks (Figure 2).
